title: Merge and merge conflicts
idea: A merge combines the work of two branches. If both changed the same lines, Git stops with a conflict and asks you to choose.

analogy.text: Two editors revise copies of one report. Edits to different paragraphs combine cleanly; a rewrite of the same sentence needs a person to choose.
analogy.breaks: Git compares lines, not meaning, so a clean merge can still be wrong.

points: `git merge feature` brings the commits of `feature` into your current branch.
If your branch has not moved, Git fast-forwards: no new commit is made.
If both branches moved, Git creates a merge commit with two parents.
To resolve a conflict, edit the file, run `git add`, then `git commit`.

steps.caption: `cheaper` branches from A and adds B. `main` still points at A.
Meanwhile `main` gets commit C. The two histories have diverged.
Merging `cheaper` creates M, a commit with two parents. If both sides edited the same lines, Git stops first.
A new branch, `docs`, adds D while `main` stands still.
Merging `docs` is a fast-forward: `main` slides to D and no merge commit is made.

code.title: A real conflict
code.caption: Real Git output. Two branches change the same line of `menu.txt`, then you resolve it.

walk.text: Create a repository with one commit on `main`.
On `cheaper`, change the price. `-a` stages changes to files Git already tracks.
Back on `main`, change the same line differently.
Both branches changed that line, so Git stops with a conflict.
`UU` flags the unmerged file. `cat` shows both versions between conflict markers.
Write the final text, stage the file, and commit to finish the merge.
The graph shows the merge commit joining both lines.

pitfalls: Do not commit the markers `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>`; search the file for them first.
Commit or stash (shelve) work before merging; `git merge --abort` may not restore uncommitted changes.
Always keeping your side silently drops a teammate's change.

quiz.q: What does the last command print?
quiz.code:
echo a > f.txt && git add f.txt && git commit -m base
git switch -c x
echo b > f.txt && git commit -am x
git switch main
echo c > f.txt && git commit -am main
git merge x
git status --short
quiz.why: Both branches changed `f.txt` from the same base, so the merge stops. `UU` marks a file with unmerged changes.

takeaway: A clean merge is automatic; a conflict means you decide what the file says.

starters: What is the difference between merge and rebase?
